title: How do you configure producers/consumers for guaranteed delivery (acks=all, retries, transactions, manual offset commit, DLQ)?
shortTitle: Configuring producers and consumers for guaranteed delivery

s1_definition.profdef: Guaranteed delivery in Kafka means a produced record is reliably persisted and eventually processed exactly once in effect, with no silent loss and no unhandled failure. You achieve it with a coordinated set of settings across the whole path: on the producer, acks=all with min.insync.replicas, enabled idempotence, effectively infinite retries with proper delivery timeout, and optionally transactions for atomic multi-write; on the consumer, manual offset commit after processing with read-committed isolation; and operationally, a dead letter queue so records that cannot be processed are isolated rather than lost or blocking. No single setting guarantees delivery; it is the combination that does.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of guaranteeing that every transfer instruction at National Bank of India is never lost and always acted upon. The producer side is like registered post with delivery confirmation: the sender keeps resending until the recipient confirms receipt (acks and retries), and the post office files a copy in multiple vaults before confirming (min in-sync replicas). The consumer side is like the clerk only stamping a form as done after actually completing the work, not when it lands on the desk (manual commit after processing). And a dead letter queue is the problem tray for forms that genuinely cannot be processed, so they are set aside for follow-up rather than lost or jamming the line.
s1_definition.oneliner: Guaranteed delivery is a stack: acks=all plus min in-sync replicas plus idempotence plus retries on the producer, manual commit after processing with read-committed on the consumer, and a dead letter queue for the unprocessable, all working together.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Guaranteed delivery in Kafka means a produced record is reliably persisted and eventually processed exactly once in effect, with no silent loss and no unhandled failure. You achieve it with a coordinated set of settings across the whole path: on the producer, acks=all with min.insync.replicas, enabled idempotence, effectively infinite retries with proper delivery timeout, and optionally transactions for atomic multi-write; on the consumer, manual offset commit after processing with read-committed isolation; and operationally, a dead letter queue so records that cannot be processed are isolated rather than lost or blocking. No single setting guarantees delivery; it is the combination that does.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of guaranteeing that every transfer instruction at National Bank of India is never lost and always acted upon. The producer side is like registered post with delivery confirmation: the sender keeps resending until the recipient confirms receipt (acks and retries), and the post office files a copy in multiple vaults before confirming (min in-sync replicas). The consumer side is like the clerk only stamping a form as done after actually completing the work, not when it lands on the desk (manual commit after processing). And a dead letter queue is the problem tray for forms that genuinely cannot be processed, so they are set aside for follow-up rather than lost or jamming the line.

**One line to remember:** Guaranteed delivery is a stack: acks=all plus min in-sync replicas plus idempotence plus retries on the producer, manual commit after processing with read-committed on the consumer, and a dead letter queue for the unprocessable, all working together.

sections.s2_technical:
Start on the producer side, because that is where records can be lost before they are even stored. You set `acks=all` so the broker only acknowledges after all in-sync replicas persist the record, and you pair it with a topic `min.insync.replicas` of at least two so acks all actually means at least two replicas, not just the leader. You enable idempotence with `enable.idempotence=true`, which is the default now, so retries never create duplicates; this requires acks all and bounded in-flight requests. You set `retries` effectively to the maximum and rely on `delivery.timeout.ms` to bound how long the producer keeps trying, so transient broker or network issues are retried automatically rather than dropping the record. If you need atomicity across several writes or exactly-once read-process-write, you add a `transactional.id` and wrap the work in begin, send, and commit.

On the consumer side, the risk is marking records as done before they are really processed. So you turn off auto-commit with `enable.auto.commit=false` and commit the offset manually only after your processing has fully succeeded, which gives at-least-once delivery and means a crash resumes from the last truly completed record. If producers use transactions, you set the consumer `isolation.level=read_committed` so it only sees committed records and skips aborted ones. In Spring Kafka you use a manual or record acknowledgment mode and call acknowledge after handling.

Operationally, some records can never be processed, like a poison pill or a permanent validation failure. Guaranteed delivery does not mean guaranteed success for a broken record; it means the record is never silently lost. So you add a dead letter queue: after bounded retries, the consumer routes the failing record, with error metadata, to a dead letter topic and commits past it, so the partition keeps flowing and the record is preserved for inspection and later redrive. You also monitor the dead letter topic, because an unwatched one becomes a silent graveyard.

The senior nuances are these. Guaranteed delivery is end to end, so a weak link anywhere, for example acks one, or auto-commit, or no dead letter queue, breaks the guarantee regardless of how strong the other links are. At-least-once plus idempotent processing is the practical shape of exactly-once for most systems, because true exactly-once requires transactions and read-committed and is more expensive. You must also make downstream side effects idempotent, keyed on a business id, so that the inevitable retries and replays do not double-apply. And you size and monitor everything: in-sync replicas, producer errors, consumer lag, and dead letter depth, because guaranteed delivery is as much an operational discipline as a set of config flags.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must never lose a transfer event and must eventually process every one. Records could be lost at produce time if the broker acknowledges too early, so the producer uses acks all with min in-sync replicas two, idempotence, and long retries. This is exactly the producer side of guaranteed delivery.

Problem 2 — Records could be marked processed before the work is done if the consumer auto-commits, so the consumer commits manually only after successful settlement and reads committed. This is exactly the consumer side.

Problem 3 — A few records are permanently broken and would otherwise block or be lost, so after bounded retries they go to a dead letter topic and the consumer advances. This is exactly the operational safety net.

We simulate the whole guaranteed-delivery path in plain Java. A `GuaranteedProducer` retries until acknowledged under an acks-all, min-in-sync check; a `GuaranteedConsumer` processes, commits manually on success, retries transient failures, and routes permanent failures to a `DeadLetterQueue`. The demo sends a record that needs retries, processes a good record with manual commit, and dead-letters a permanently failing one. The code will show: a `TransferEvent`, the `GuaranteedProducer`, the `GuaranteedConsumer`, a `DeadLetterQueue`, and a demo.

```yaml
# application.yml — full guaranteed-delivery configuration
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      acks: all                                  # all in-sync replicas must persist
      retries: 2147483647                        # retry transient failures
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true                 # no duplicates on retry
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5
        delivery.timeout.ms: 120000              # bound total retry time
      transaction-id-prefix: tx-transfer-        # optional: atomic multi-write
    consumer:
      enable-auto-commit: false                  # manual commit AFTER processing
      isolation-level: read_committed            # only committed records
    listener:
      ack-mode: MANUAL
# Topic: min.insync.replicas=2, replication-factor=3
# DefaultErrorHandler + DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer with FixedBackOff(1000, 3)
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one transfer T1 produced while the in-sync set briefly dips, then consumed, a duplicate of T1, and a permanently bad transfer T2.

Step 1: The producer sends T1 with acks all and min in-sync two. On the first two attempts the in-sync set is only one, below the minimum, so the broker would reject and the producer retries rather than dropping the record. On the third attempt the in-sync set has recovered to three, so the write is acknowledged, safely on all in-sync replicas. No record was lost despite the dip.

Step 2: The consumer receives T1 at offset 100, processes it successfully, records its id for idempotency, and only then commits offset 100. Because the commit is manual and after processing, a crash before this point would have reprocessed T1 rather than skipping it.

Step 3: The consumer receives T1 again at offset 101, a duplicate from an at-least-once redelivery. It recognizes the id as already processed and skips it, advancing the offset without double-settling, which is the idempotency that makes at-least-once safe.

Step 4: The consumer receives T2 at offset 102, which is permanently bad. Processing throws, and because it is classified permanent, the consumer does not waste retries; it publishes T2 with the reason to the dead letter queue and commits past offset 102, so the partition keeps flowing and the record is preserved rather than lost.

Step 5: At the end, T1 was delivered and processed exactly once in effect, the duplicate was safely ignored, T2 is isolated in the dead letter queue for inspection and later redrive, and the committed offset reflects real completed and resolved work. Nothing was silently lost at any stage.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  PRODUCER (guaranteed persist)
    send(acks=all) → ISR<2? retry ... → ISR>=2 → persist all replicas → ACK
    enable.idempotence → retries never duplicate
         │
         ▼
  Kafka topic (RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2) — durable
         │
         ▼
  CONSUMER (guaranteed process)
    poll → process
      ├─ success → idempotent record id → MANUAL COMMIT (after work)
      ├─ duplicate id → skip (at-least-once made safe)
      ├─ transient fail → retry (bounded)
      └─ permanent / exhausted → DLQ + commit past
         │
         ▼
  DLQ (monitored) → inspect → redrive after fix
  read_committed: only see committed records (with transactions)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Guaranteed delivery in Kafka is not one setting; it is a coordinated stack across the whole path, and the key insight is that any weak link breaks the guarantee. On the producer I set acks all so the broker only acknowledges after all in-sync replicas persist the record, and I pair it with a topic min in-sync replicas of at least two so acks all actually means at least two replicas rather than just the leader. I enable idempotence, which is the default, so retries never create duplicates, and I set retries effectively to the maximum bounded by the delivery timeout so transient broker or network issues are retried automatically instead of dropping the record. When I need atomicity across several writes or exactly-once read-process-write, I add a transactional id and wrap the work in begin, send, and commit.

On the consumer the risk is marking records done before they are really processed, so I turn off auto-commit and commit the offset manually only after processing has fully succeeded, which gives at-least-once delivery and means a crash resumes from the last truly completed record. If the producers use transactions, I set the consumer to read committed so it only sees committed records and skips aborted ones. Because at-least-once can redeliver, I make the processing idempotent on a business id, so a replayed record is recognized and skipped rather than double-applied.

Operationally I accept that guaranteed delivery does not mean guaranteed success for a broken record; it means a record is never silently lost. So after bounded retries, a record that cannot be processed, a poison pill or a permanent validation failure, is routed to a dead letter topic with error metadata and the consumer commits past it, keeping the partition flowing and preserving the record for inspection and later redrive. And I monitor everything, the in-sync replicas, producer errors, consumer lag, and dead letter depth, because guaranteed delivery is as much operational discipline as configuration.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, the transfers path uses exactly this stack: producers run acks all with min in-sync two on a replication-factor-three topic, idempotence on, and long retries, so a brief in-sync dip causes retries, not loss. The settlement consumer commits manually after successful settlement, reads committed, and is idempotent on the trade id so redeliveries never double-settle, and permanently bad records go to a monitored dead letter topic for redrive. The senior framing I give is that guaranteed delivery is end to end, and the practical shape of it for most banking systems is at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing plus a dead letter queue, reserving full transactions for the places that truly need atomic multi-write, because the guarantee is only as strong as its weakest configured link.

keyPoints: At-most-once: fire and forget — may lose messages
At-least-once: retry on failure — may duplicate
